text.title: Araby
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: A young boy living on North Richmond Street in Dublin becomes infatuated with his neighbor Mangan's sister and promises to bring her a gift from the Araby bazaar, but arrives too late and leaves empty-handed, experiencing a moment of self-recognition and disillusionment.

rootSpan.title: Araby
rootSpan.description: A young boy living on North Richmond Street in Dublin becomes infatuated with his neighbor Mangan's sister and promises to bring her a gift from the Araby bazaar, but arrives too late and leaves empty-handed, experiencing a moment of self-recognition and disillusionment.

childSpans.title: Setting and Infatuation
childSpans.description: Introduction to North Richmond Street, the boy's house, and the emergence of his obsession with Mangan's sister

childSpans.title: North Richmond Street and the House
childSpans.description: Description of the blind street, the uninhabited house, and the books left by the former priest tenant

childSpans.title: Street Introduction
childSpans.description: North Richmond Street is described as blind and quiet except when school lets out

childSpans.title: The House
childSpans.description: The uninhabited two-storey house at the blind end of the street

childSpans.title: Books and the Former Tenant
childSpans.description: Discovery of books left by the former priest tenant and details of his charitable nature

childSpans.title: Winter Play and First Sight of Mangan's Sister
childSpans.description: Winter arrives, the boys play in the streets and lanes, and the narrator first observes Mangan's sister

childSpans.title: Winter Arrives
childSpans.description: Short winter days bring early dusk and cold air

childSpans.title: Play in the Streets and Lanes
childSpans.description: The boys play through dark muddy lanes, encountering rough tribes and exploring gardens and stables

childSpans.title: Mangan's Sister Appears
childSpans.description: The boys hide from the uncle and watch Mangan's sister call her brother in to tea; the narrator observes her closely

childSpans.title: The Obsession Begins
childSpans.description: The narrator begins watching Mangan's sister every morning and becomes consumed by thoughts of her

childSpans.title: Morning Vigil
childSpans.description: The narrator lies on the parlour floor watching her door, unable to be seen

childSpans.title: Following Her
childSpans.description: The narrator follows her each morning, quickening his pace to pass her, never having spoken to her

childSpans.title: Romantic Obsession
childSpans.description: Her image accompanies him everywhere; her name becomes a summons to his blood

childSpans.title: The Promise
childSpans.description: The narrator encounters Mangan's sister, she mentions the Araby bazaar, and he promises to bring her something

childSpans.title: Market Day and Romantic Fantasy
childSpans.description: The narrator accompanies his aunt to the market and imagines himself as a knight bearing a chalice through foes

childSpans.title: Walking Through the Market
childSpans.description: The narrator walks through flaring streets with his aunt, surrounded by drunken men, bargaining women, and street singers

childSpans.title: Chalice Fantasy
childSpans.description: He imagines bearing a chalice safely through a throng of foes; her name springs to his lips in strange prayers

childSpans.title: The Back Drawing-Room
childSpans.description: The narrator enters the dark back drawing-room where the priest died and experiences an emotional moment

childSpans.title: In the Dark Room
childSpans.description: A dark rainy evening; the narrator presses his palms together and murmurs 'O love! O love!' repeatedly

childSpans.title: First Conversation with Mangan's Sister
childSpans.description: Mangan's sister finally speaks to the narrator, mentions the Araby bazaar, and he promises to bring her something

childSpans.title: She Speaks
childSpans.description: Mangan's sister addresses the narrator for the first time; he is confused and cannot answer properly

childSpans.title: The Araby Bazaar
childSpans.description: She asks if he is going to Araby; she says it would be splendid but cannot go due to a convent retreat

childSpans.title: The Promise
childSpans.description: The narrator promises to bring her something from the bazaar if he goes

childSpans.title: Anticipation and Delay
childSpans.description: The narrator becomes consumed by thoughts of the bazaar and struggles through school and home life waiting for Saturday

childSpans.title: Obsession Intensifies
childSpans.description: The narrator is consumed by thoughts of Araby and struggles to focus on school and daily life

childSpans.title: Innumerable Follies
childSpans.description: The narrator wishes to annihilate the intervening days; her image comes between him and his studies

childSpans.title: School Struggles
childSpans.description: The narrator cannot focus in class; his master watches his face pass from amiability to sternness

childSpans.title: Permission Requested
childSpans.description: The narrator asks for leave to go to the bazaar on Saturday night; his aunt is surprised

childSpans.title: Saturday Morning
childSpans.description: Saturday morning arrives; the narrator reminds his uncle of his intention to go to the bazaar

childSpans.title: Reminding Uncle
childSpans.description: The narrator reminds his uncle he wishes to go to the bazaar; the uncle answers curtly

childSpans.title: Bad Humour
childSpans.description: Unable to watch from the parlour window, the narrator leaves the house in bad humour and walks to school

childSpans.title: Waiting and Delay
childSpans.description: The narrator returns home to dinner, waits for his uncle, and endures Mrs Mercer's visit

childSpans.title: Waiting and Wandering
childSpans.description: The narrator stares at the clock, then wanders the upper rooms, singing and looking out at Mangan's house

childSpans.title: Mrs Mercer's Visit
childSpans.description: Mrs Mercer, a pawnbroker's widow, sits at the fire; the meal is prolonged and the uncle does not arrive

childSpans.title: Uncle Arrives Late
childSpans.description: At nine o'clock the uncle arrives home, having forgotten to give the narrator money for the bazaar

childSpans.title: The Bazaar
childSpans.description: The narrator finally receives money, travels to the Araby bazaar, but arrives too late and leaves empty-handed

childSpans.title: Getting the Money
childSpans.description: The aunt persuades the uncle to give the narrator money; the uncle recites poetry before the narrator leaves

childSpans.title: Aunt's Intervention
childSpans.description: The aunt energetically persuades the uncle to give the narrator money and let him go

childSpans.title: Money Received
childSpans.description: The uncle gives the narrator a florin and apologizes for forgetting

childSpans.title: Uncle Recites Poetry
childSpans.description: The uncle asks if the narrator knows 'The Arab's Farewell to his Steed' and begins to recite it

childSpans.title: Journey to the Bazaar
childSpans.description: The narrator travels by train to the Araby bazaar, arriving near closing time

childSpans.title: Walk to Station
childSpans.description: The narrator holds a florin tightly and strides down Buckingham Street towards the station

childSpans.title: Train Journey
childSpans.description: The narrator takes a third-class carriage on a deserted train that moves slowly through ruinous houses and over the river

childSpans.title: Arrival at Bazaar
childSpans.description: The train arrives at Westland Row Station; the narrator sees by a clock that it is ten minutes to ten

childSpans.title: Inside the Bazaar
childSpans.description: The narrator enters the bazaar, finds it nearly closed, and encounters a young lady at a stall

childSpans.title: Entering the Bazaar
childSpans.description: The narrator passes through a turnstile, paying a shilling; nearly all stalls are closed and the hall is mostly dark

childSpans.title: Examining Stalls
childSpans.description: The narrator walks to a stall and examines porcelain vases and flowered tea-sets

childSpans.title: Young Lady at the Stall
childSpans.description: A young lady with an English accent asks if the narrator wishes to buy anything; he declines and lingers before leaving

childSpans.title: Epiphany and Disillusionment
childSpans.description: The narrator realizes the bazaar is closing and experiences a moment of self-recognition and anguish

childSpans.title: Lights Out
childSpans.description: A voice calls that the light is out; the upper part of the hall becomes completely dark

childSpans.title: Self-Recognition
childSpans.description: Gazing into the darkness, the narrator sees himself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; his eyes burn with anguish and anger

data.physicalDescription: Brown figure, soft rope of hair, dress that swings as she moves, white curve of neck, white border of petticoat

two-young-gentlemen.name: Two Young Gentlemen
two-young-gentlemen.description: Two young men with English accents who flirt with the young lady at the bazaar stall

train-station.context: The departure point for the narrator's journey to the bazaar

e01-street-description.description: North Richmond Street is described as a blind street that is quiet except when the Christian Brothers' School lets the boys free

e02-house-description.description: An uninhabited two-storey house stands at the blind end of the street, detached from its neighbors; the other houses gaze at one another with brown imperturbable faces

e03-books-discovery.description: The narrator finds paper-covered books left by the former priest tenant in the waste room: The Abbot, The Devout Communicant, and The Memoirs of Vidocq; he also finds a rusty bicycle-pump in the wild garden

e04-winter-arrival.description: Winter arrives with short days and early dusk; the houses grow sombre and the sky becomes the colour of ever-changing violet

e05-play-in-streets.description: The boys play in the dark muddy lanes behind the houses, running the gauntlet of rough tribes from the cottages, exploring dark dripping gardens and dark odorous stables where a coachman works with a horse

e06-mangans-sister-first-appearance.description: The boys hide from the uncle when he is seen turning the corner; when Mangan's sister comes out on the doorstep to call her brother in to tea, they watch her from the shadow; her brother teases her and the narrator stands by the railings looking at her

e07-morning-watching.description: Every morning the narrator lies on the floor in the front parlour with the blind pulled down to within an inch of the sash so he cannot be seen; when Mangan's sister comes out on the doorstep his heart leaps

e08-following-her.description: The narrator follows Mangan's sister each morning, keeping her brown figure in his eye; when their ways diverge he quickens his pace and passes her; he has never spoken to her except for a few casual words

e09-romantic-obsession.description: Her image accompanies the narrator everywhere; her name becomes like a summons to all his foolish blood; his body is like a harp and her words and gestures are like fingers running upon the wires

e10-market-day.description: On Saturday evenings when his aunt goes marketing, the narrator carries parcels through flaring streets with drunken men, bargaining women, labourers, shop-boys, and street-singers singing about O'Donovan Rossa and troubles in their native land

e11-chalice-fantasy.description: The narrator imagines that he bears a chalice safely through a throng of foes; her name springs to his lips in strange prayers and praises which he does not understand; his eyes are often full of tears and a flood from his heart seems to pour itself out

e12-back-drawing-room.description: One dark rainy evening the narrator goes into the back drawing-room where the priest died; he hears rain impinge upon the earth through broken panes; he presses the palms of his hands together until they tremble, murmuring 'O love! O love!' many times

e13-first-words.description: Mangan's sister finally speaks to the narrator; he is so confused that he does not know what to answer

e14-araby-mentioned.description: Mangan's sister asks if the narrator is going to Araby; she says it would be a splendid bazaar and she would love to go; she cannot go because there will be a retreat that week in her convent; while she speaks she turns a silver bracelet round and round her wrist

e15-promise-made.description: The narrator promises that if he goes to Araby, he will bring Mangan's sister something

e16-araby-obsession.description: Innumerable follies lay waste the narrator's waking and sleeping thoughts after the evening; he wishes to annihilate the tedious intervening days; the syllables of the word Araby are called to him through the silence and cast an Eastern enchantment over him

e17-school-struggles.description: The narrator cannot focus in class; her image comes between him and the page he strives to read; his master's face passes from amiability to sternness; he answers few questions and has hardly any patience with the serious work of life

e18-permission-requested.description: The narrator asks for leave to go to the bazaar on Saturday night; his aunt is surprised and hopes it is not some Freemason affair

e19-saturday-reminder.description: On Saturday morning the narrator reminds his uncle that he wishes to go to the bazaar in the evening; the uncle is fussing at the hallstand looking for the hat-brush and answers curtly

e20-uncle-curtly-agrees.description: Unable to go into the front parlour and lie at the window because his uncle is in the hall, the narrator leaves the house in bad humour and walks slowly towards the school; the air is pitilessly raw and his heart misgives him

e21-waiting-for-uncle.description: When the narrator comes home to dinner his uncle has not yet been home; he sits staring at the clock and then mounts the staircase to the upper part of the house; he goes from room to room singing and looks out the front window at his companions playing below and at the dark house where she lived

e22-mrs-mercer-visit.description: Mrs Mercer, an old garrulous woman and pawnbroker's widow who collects used stamps for pious purposes, sits at the fire; the meal is prolonged beyond an hour and the uncle does not come; Mrs Mercer leaves after eight o'clock because she does not like to be out late as the night air is bad for her

e23-uncle-arrives-late.description: At nine o'clock the narrator hears his uncle's latchkey in the halldoor; the uncle is talking to himself and the hallstand rocks when it receives the weight of his overcoat; when the uncle is midway through his dinner the narrator asks for money to go to the bazaar; the uncle has forgotten

e24-aunt-persuades.description: The aunt says energetically to the uncle: 'Can't you give him the money and let him go? You've kept him late enough as it is.'

e25-money-given.description: The uncle says he is very sorry he has forgotten and gives the narrator money; the uncle says he believes in the old saying 'All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy'

e26-uncle-recites.description: The uncle asks the narrator if he knows 'The Arab's Farewell to his Steed' and when the narrator leaves the kitchen the uncle is about to recite the opening lines to the aunt

e27-walk-to-station.description: The narrator holds a florin tightly in his hand and strides down Buckingham Street towards the station; the sight of the streets thronged with buyers and glaring with gas recalls to him the purpose of his journey

e28-train-journey.description: The narrator takes his seat in a third-class carriage of a deserted train; after an intolerable delay the train moves out of the station slowly, creeping onward among ruinous houses and over the twinkling river

e29-arrival-at-bazaar.description: At Westland Row Station a crowd of people presses to the carriage doors but the porters move them back saying it is a special train for the bazaar; the narrator remains alone in the bare carriage; in a few minutes the train draws up beside an improvised wooden platform; the narrator passes out onto the road and sees by the lighted dial of a clock that it is ten minutes to ten

e30-entering-bazaar.description: The narrator cannot find any sixpenny entrance and fearing the bazaar will be closed passes in quickly through a turnstile, handing a shilling to a weary-looking man; he finds himself in a big hall girdled at half its height by a gallery; nearly all the stalls are closed and the greater part of the hall is in darkness; he recognizes a silence like that which pervades a church after a service

e31-stall-examination.description: The narrator walks into the centre of the bazaar timidly; a few people are gathered about the stalls which are still open; before a curtain over which the words Café Chantant are written in coloured lamps, two men are counting money on a salver; the narrator goes over to one of the stalls and examines porcelain vases and flowered tea-sets

e32-young-lady-encounter.description: At the door of the stall a young lady is talking and laughing with two young gentlemen with English accents; the narrator remarks their English accents and listens vaguely to their conversation; observing the narrator the young lady comes over and asks if he wishes to buy anything; the tone of her voice is not encouraging; she seems to have spoken out of a sense of duty; the narrator looks humbly at the great jars and murmurs 'No, thank you'; the young lady changes the position of one of the vases and goes back to the two young men; they begin to talk of the same subject; once or twice the young lady glances at the narrator over her shoulder

e33-lights-out.description: The narrator lingers before the stall though he knows his stay is useless; he turns away slowly and walks down the middle of the bazaar; he allows the two pennies to fall against the sixpence in his pocket; he hears a voice call from one end of the gallery that the light is out; the upper part of the hall is now completely dark

e34-self-recognition.description: Gazing up into the darkness the narrator sees himself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; his eyes burn with anguish and anger

rel-boy-mangans-sister.description: The narrator is infatuated with Mangan's sister; he watches her obsessively, follows her, and promises to bring her a gift from the bazaar

rel-boy-aunt.description: The narrator lives with his aunt who advocates for him to go to the bazaar

rel-mangans-sister-mangan.description: Mangan's sister and her brother Mangan live together; he teases her

rel-uncle-aunt.description: The uncle and aunt live together in the narrator's house

Formalist Reading of Araby.name: Formalist Reading of Araby
Formalist Reading of Araby.description: A formalist interpretation focusing on narrative structure, point of view, symbolism, and the formal properties of language and composition. Emphasizes how Joyce's stylistic choices—particularly the use of free indirect discourse, imagery patterns, and structural parallelism—create meaning through form rather than external reference.

theme-illusion-vs-reality.name: Illusion versus Reality
theme-illusion-vs-reality.description: The tension between the narrator's romanticized fantasy and the mundane, disappointing reality he encounters. Formalist analysis reveals how Joyce uses language registers and imagery to mark the gap between the narrator's inner world and external fact.

theme-narrative-unreliability.name: Narrative Unreliability and Self-Deception
theme-narrative-unreliability.description: The narrator's inability to see himself clearly, constructed through Joyce's use of free indirect discourse that allows the reader to perceive the narrator's self-deception even as he experiences it. The form itself enacts the theme.

theme-epiphany-through-form.name: Epiphany as Formal Revelation
theme-epiphany-through-form.description: The final moment of self-recognition structured as a formal epiphany—a sudden illumination achieved through the narrative's formal architecture. The shift from darkness to self-awareness is a structural achievement.

theme-language-and-desire.name: Language as Mediator of Desire
theme-language-and-desire.description: How the narrator's desire is constructed and sustained through language—the 'syllables' of Araby, the incantatory quality of her name, the poetic registers that elevate mundane experience. Language creates the object of desire.

sym-araby.name: Araby
sym-araby.description: The bazaar functions as a formal symbol whose meaning is entirely constructed through language and narrative expectation. Its 'Eastern enchantment' exists only in the narrator's linguistic imagination; the actual bazaar is a formal disappointment that mirrors the narrator's self-deception.

currentMeanings.description: Romantic escape and transcendence (in the narrator's imagination)
The gap between signifier and signified

sym-light-darkness.name: Light and Darkness
sym-light-darkness.description: A formal pattern of illumination and obscurity that structures the narrative. The story moves from winter darkness through anticipatory brightness to the final darkness of the bazaar, where the narrator achieves illumination through darkness—a formal paradox.

currentMeanings.description: The failure of vision and understanding

sym-chalice.name: The Chalice
sym-chalice.description: A formal symbol of the narrator's attempt to elevate mundane desire into sacred quest. The chalice imagery (religious, literary, Arthurian) reveals how the narrator uses high cultural language to construct meaning around his infatuation. The symbol's failure is the failure of this linguistic elevation.

currentMeanings.description: The inadequacy of literary forms to contain lived experience

sym-silver-bracelet.name: The Silver Bracelet
sym-silver-bracelet.description: A formal detail that marks the moment of transition from fantasy to reality. The bracelet's material specificity—silver, turning round and round—grounds the narrator's fantasy in concrete sensory detail, yet this very concreteness makes the fantasy more powerful and more delusional.

currentMeanings.description: The power of concrete detail in constructing illusion

sym-blind-street.name: The Blind Street
sym-blind-street.description: A formal opening image that establishes the narrative's concern with vision and blindness. The 'blind' street (a dead end) is the formal correlative of the narrator's moral and perceptual blindness. The street's closure mirrors the narrative's closure in self-recognition.

currentMeanings.description: The inescapability of the narrator's condition

symrel-araby-chalice.name: Araby as Failed Chalice
symrel-araby-chalice.description: The bazaar is the formal realization of the chalice fantasy. Its failure to deliver transcendence reveals the inadequacy of the narrator's linguistic and imaginative constructions. The relationship is one of formal irony.
symrel-araby-chalice.nature: The actual bazaar exposes the chalice fantasy as self-deception constructed through language. The formal gap between expectation and reality is the story's central concern.
symrel-araby-chalice.interpretation: The actual bazaar exposes the chalice fantasy as self-deception constructed through language. The formal gap between expectation and reality is the story's central concern.

symrel-darkness-vision.name: Darkness as True Vision
symrel-darkness-vision.description: The final darkness of the bazaar paradoxically brings true vision—self-recognition. This formal inversion suggests that the narrator's previous 'illumination' (his romantic fantasy) was actually blindness.
symrel-darkness-vision.nature: The narrative structure moves from false light (romantic idealization) to true darkness (self-knowledge). Vision and blindness are formally inverted.
symrel-darkness-vision.interpretation: The narrative structure moves from false light (romantic idealization) to true darkness (self-knowledge). Vision and blindness are formally inverted.

symrel-blind-street-narrator.name: Blind Street as Narrator's Condition
symrel-blind-street-narrator.description: The blind street is the formal objective correlative of the narrator's blindness to himself. The street's closure at both ends mirrors the narrator's inability to escape his own self-deception.
symrel-blind-street-narrator.nature: The setting formally enacts the narrator's psychological condition. The street's dead-end structure is replicated in the narrative's circular return to the starting point of self-recognition.
symrel-blind-street-narrator.interpretation: The setting formally enacts the narrator's psychological condition. The street's dead-end structure is replicated in the narrative's circular return to the starting point of self-recognition.

symrel-bracelet-language.name: Bracelet as Linguistic Crystallization
symrel-bracelet-language.description: The silver bracelet represents the moment when abstract desire becomes concretely embodied in language and perception. Its turning motion formalizes the narrator's obsessive return to the object of desire.
symrel-bracelet-language.nature: The bracelet's material specificity demonstrates how language and perception construct the object of desire. The formal detail creates the emotional intensity.
symrel-bracelet-language.interpretation: The bracelet's material specificity demonstrates how language and perception construct the object of desire. The formal detail creates the emotional intensity.

narrator.name: The Boy-Narrator (Retrospective)
narrator.description: A retrospective first-person narrator recounting his childhood experience with mature ironic distance. Joyce employs free indirect discourse to blur the boundary between the narrator's youthful consciousness and his adult understanding, allowing the reader to perceive the narrator's self-deception even as it unfolds. The narrative voice is formally unreliable—it enacts the very blindness it eventually recognizes.

reader.name: The Formalist Reader
reader.description: A reader attuned to narrative structure, point of view, imagery patterns, and the formal properties of language. This reader recognizes that meaning is constructed through the story's formal architecture—the gap between the narrator's language and his understanding, the patterns of light and darkness, the movement from blindness to vision. The reader perceives irony through formal analysis rather than thematic statement.

author.name: James Joyce
author.description: A modernist craftsman concerned with the formal properties of narrative consciousness. Joyce uses free indirect discourse, precise imagery, and structural parallelism to create meaning. The story's form—its movement from enclosed domestic space to the bazaar's darkness, its use of religious and literary language to elevate mundane desire—is inseparable from its meaning. Joyce's formal innovation allows the reader to experience the narrator's self-deception as a formal phenomenon.

e01-street-description.note: Formal opening that establishes the 'blind' street as the objective correlative of the narrator's blindness. The description's precision and the paradox of a 'blind' street set up the narrative's concern with vision and perception.

e02-house-description.note: Continues the formal establishment of setting. The houses' 'brown imperturbable faces' and the detached house establish the spatial isolation that will contain the narrator's fantasy.

e03-books-discovery.note: Introduces the literary and religious language that will structure the narrator's fantasy. The books (The Abbot, The Devout Communicant, Memoirs of Vidocq) establish the cultural register through which the narrator will construct meaning.

e04-winter-arrival.note: Formal establishment of the light-darkness pattern. Winter's darkness and the 'ever-changing violet' sky create the atmospheric conditions for the narrator's romantic fantasy.

e05-play-in-streets.note: Establishes the mundane reality against which the narrator's fantasy will be measured. The 'dark muddy lanes' and 'dark odorous stables' create the sensory world the narrator will attempt to transcend.

e06-mangans-sister-first-appearance.note: Pivotal formal moment where the object of desire is introduced. The narrator's perspective—watching from shadow—establishes the formal pattern of observation and distance that structures the narrative.

e07-morning-watching.note: Establishes the formal pattern of the narrator's obsessive watching. The blind pulled down 'within an inch' creates a formal frame that mediates perception and desire.

e08-following-her.note: Continues the formal pattern of pursuit and distance. The narrator's quickening pace and passing her establishes the dynamic of approach and retreat that structures his desire.

e09-romantic-obsession.note: Crucial formal moment where the narrator's desire is expressed through elevated language—'harp,' 'wires,' 'summons.' The free indirect discourse allows the reader to perceive the narrator's self-aggrandizement through language.

e10-market-day.note: Establishes the sensory and social reality of Dublin. The market's noise and commerce provide formal contrast to the narrator's romantic fantasy.

e11-chalice-fantasy.note: Formally crucial moment where the narrator's desire reaches its most elevated expression. The chalice imagery, the 'strange prayers,' and the tears reveal how the narrator uses religious and literary language to construct meaning. This is the apex of his self-deception.

e12-back-drawing-room.note: Formal intensification of the narrator's emotional state. The dark room, the rain, the trembling hands, and the repeated 'O love!' create a formally heightened moment of emotional expression.

e13-first-words.note: Pivotal formal moment where the narrator's fantasy meets reality. His confusion and inability to respond reveal the gap between his inner world and his capacity for actual communication.

e14-araby-mentioned.note: Formally crucial—the word 'Araby' enters the narrative and becomes the focal point of the narrator's desire. The silver bracelet's concrete detail grounds the fantasy in sensory perception. This moment crystallizes the narrator's quest.

e15-promise-made.note: The promise formalizes the narrator's commitment to the quest. The brevity of this dialogue contrasts with the elaborate fantasy it generates, revealing the gap between action and imagination.

e16-araby-obsession.note: Formally crucial revelation where the narrator's obsession reaches its peak. The 'syllables' of Araby, the 'Eastern enchantment,' and the 'innumerable follies' reveal how language constructs desire. The free indirect discourse allows the reader to perceive the narrator's self-deception.

e17-school-struggles.note: Demonstrates the narrator's inability to function in the mundane world. The master's face moving from 'amiability to sternness' formalizes the conflict between fantasy and reality.

e18-permission-requested.note: Moves the narrative toward the bazaar. The aunt's suspicion about 'Freemason affair' introduces an ironic note about the narrator's quest.

e19-saturday-reminder.note: Establishes the Saturday evening as the formal deadline. The uncle's curtness introduces the obstacle that will delay the narrator's quest.

e20-uncle-curtly-agrees.note: The narrator's bad humour and the 'pitilessly raw' air establish the formal tone of disappointment and frustration that will intensify.

e21-waiting-for-uncle.note: Formally crucial moment of suspense and anticipation. The narrator's movement through the house, his singing, and his looking out at Mangan's house create a formally heightened state of expectation.

e22-mrs-mercer-visit.note: The prolonged meal and Mrs. Mercer's departure after eight o'clock intensify the formal tension. The delay becomes a formal obstacle to the narrator's quest.

e23-uncle-arrives-late.note: The uncle's late arrival and initial forgetfulness create formal suspense. The narrator's request for money and the uncle's forgetfulness establish the central obstacle.

e24-aunt-persuades.note: The aunt's intervention is formally crucial—she advocates for the narrator's quest. Her direct speech contrasts with the narrator's indirect, fantasy-laden consciousness.

e25-money-given.note: The florin is given, and the uncle's proverb about work and play provides an ironic commentary on the narrator's quest. The money is the formal enabler of the journey.

e26-uncle-recites.note: The uncle's recitation of 'The Arab's Farewell to his Steed' provides formal irony—the uncle's poetry about leaving the beloved parallels the narrator's quest, but with a different emotional register.

e27-walk-to-station.note: The narrator's purposeful stride and the florin held tightly establish the formal momentum toward the bazaar. The 'glaring' streets recall the market day and ground the fantasy in sensory reality.

e28-train-journey.note: The train's slow movement through 'ruinous houses' and over the 'twinkling river' creates a formally heightened journey. The deserted carriage emphasizes the narrator's isolation.

e29-arrival-at-bazaar.note: The arrival at Westland Row and the clock showing 'ten minutes to ten' establish the formal urgency. The crowd and the special train create a sense of occasion that contrasts with the bazaar's actual condition.

e30-entering-bazaar.note: Formally crucial—the narrator enters the bazaar and discovers it is closing. The darkness, the closed stalls, and the silence 'like that which pervades a church after a service' create formal irony. The bazaar is a disappointment.

e31-stall-examination.note: The narrator's timid examination of the porcelain vases and tea-sets reveals his uncertainty. The formal detail of the 'Café Chantant' and the men counting money establish the bazaar's commercial reality.

e32-young-lady-encounter.note: Formally crucial moment where the narrator encounters another figure of desire—the young lady with the English accent. Her indifference and the two young gentlemen's flirtation create formal irony. The narrator's 'No, thank you' is a formal moment of renunciation.

e33-lights-out.note: Formally crucial—the lights go out, and the bazaar becomes completely dark. The narrator's lingering and the coins falling in his pocket create formal tension. The darkness is the formal condition for the epiphany.

e34-self-recognition.note: The climactic epiphany where the narrator sees himself 'as a creature driven and derided by vanity.' This is the formal culmination of the narrative—the moment where the narrator achieves the vision that has been denied him throughout. The eyes burning with 'anguish and anger' mark the formal intensity of self-recognition.

boy.note: The protagonist and narrator whose consciousness structures the entire narrative. His unreliability and self-deception are the formal subject of the story.

mangans-sister.note: The object of desire whose actual presence is minimal but whose imagined presence dominates the narrative. She is constructed entirely through the narrator's language and perception.

uncle.note: The formal obstacle who delays the narrator's quest. His forgetfulness and his recitation of poetry provide ironic commentary on the narrator's romantic fantasy.

aunt.note: The practical advocate who enables the narrator's quest. Her direct speech contrasts with the narrator's elaborate fantasy.

mangan.note: The brother whose teasing establishes the social context for the narrator's infatuation. He is a minor formal element.

priest.note: The former tenant whose books and bicycle-pump establish the literary and material context for the narrator's fantasy. His death in the back drawing-room creates the formal setting for the narrator's emotional intensification.

mrs-mercer.note: The gossipy neighbor whose visit delays the narrator's quest. She represents the mundane social reality that contrasts with the narrator's fantasy.

young-lady-bazaar.note: A formal mirror of Mangan's sister. Her indifference and English accent create ironic contrast with the narrator's expectations. She represents the actual world's indifference to the narrator's fantasy.

school-master.note: The authority figure whose stern face marks the narrator's inability to function in the mundane world. He represents the conflict between fantasy and reality.

two-young-gentlemen.note: The flirtatious young men who represent a more successful form of social engagement. Their ease with the young lady contrasts with the narrator's awkwardness.

companions.note: The other boys who provide the social context for the narrator's infatuation. They are a formal collective rather than individual characters.

coachman.note: A minor figure who represents the working world. He is part of the sensory reality that the narrator attempts to transcend.

abs-quest-to-araby.note: The central formal structure of the narrative. The quest organizes all the events and creates the narrative's forward momentum. Its failure is the story's formal subject.

abs-romantic-love.note: The narrator's desire to express romantic love is never fulfilled. The absence of actual communication with Mangan's sister is formally crucial—it allows the narrator's fantasy to flourish unchecked.

abs-escape-from-reality.note: The narrator's desire to escape the mundane world through romantic fantasy structures the narrative's formal tension. The bazaar represents the formal failure of this escape.

abs-self-recognition.note: The narrator's eventual self-recognition is the formal culmination of the narrative. The absence of self-knowledge throughout the story makes the final epiphany formally significant.
